questions.q: What is OpenID Connect (OIDC) in relation to OAuth 2.0?
options: A completely separate, competing protocol
An identity layer built on top of OAuth 2.0's authorization flows
A replacement for SAML with no relation to OAuth
A Salesforce-only proprietary extension
questions.explain: OIDC adds a standardized identity layer on top of OAuth 2.0. Requesting the `openid` scope alongside OAuth scopes causes an ID token to be issued in addition to the access token.

questions.q: What does an ID token prove that a plain OAuth access token does not?
options: Which API endpoints can be called
How long the token has been cached
Who the user actually is, via identity claims like subject, email, and issuer
Which connected app created the token
questions.explain: An access token authorizes API calls; an ID token, always formatted as a JWT, carries identity claims that prove who the authenticated user is.

questions.q: Where in Setup would you configure Salesforce to trust an external OpenID Connect issuer, such as a corporate identity system?
options: Session Settings
Auth. Providers
Permission Set Groups
Login IP Ranges
questions.explain: The Auth. Providers page in Setup is where you register trust in an external authentication source, including providers using the OpenID Connect provider type.

questions.q: A client wants Salesforce to authenticate users via Google Sign-In. What's the typical scope needed to make Google return identity information, not just API access?
options: api
refresh_token
openid
full
questions.explain: Requesting the `openid` scope is what causes an OIDC-compliant provider like Google to return an ID token carrying identity claims, in addition to any OAuth access token.

questions.q: When might an architect still choose SAML over OpenID Connect for a new enterprise SSO integration?
options: SAML should always be chosen over OIDC regardless of circumstances
When integrating with a long-established enterprise identity system built around SAML, where that's the path of least resistance
SAML is never an appropriate choice anymore
Only when the client specifically forbids the use of JSON
questions.explain: Many large enterprise identity deployments predate OIDC and are built around SAML; integrating with that existing infrastructure on its own terms is often more practical than forcing a protocol switch.
